title: The Lesson I Learned From David Asking One Question
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From David Asking One Question
One question changed a battlefield, exposed a nation’s fear, revealed a forgotten God, and still confronts every believer today.
There are moments in Scripture that feel less like ancient history and more like a mirror.
This is one of them.
I have read the story of David and Goliath countless times. I knew about the giant. I knew about the sling. I knew about the victory.
But one day, I stopped looking at the giant.
I stopped looking at David.
And I started looking at a question.
A single question.
A question so simple that most people read right past it.
Yet that question exposed fear, unbelief, compromise, and spiritual paralysis all at once.
That question was:
"Who is this uncircumcised Philistine that he should defy the armies of the living God?" (1 Samuel 17:26)
The moment I truly understood that question, I realized David was seeing something nobody else could see.
The battlefield was filled with soldiers.
Experienced warriors.
Trained fighters.
Men who knew combat far better than a shepherd boy.
Yet for forty days they stood frozen.
Every morning Goliath appeared.
Every morning fear returned.
Every morning faith disappeared.
Scripture says:
"For forty days the Philistine came forward and took his stand, morning and evening" (1 Samuel 17:16).
Forty days.
Not one volunteer.
Not one challenge.
Not one act of courage.
The giant never became stronger.
The soldiers simply became more afraid.
And fear has a way of doing that.
Fear magnifies problems.
Fear enlarges obstacles.
Fear makes giants appear invincible.
Fear makes God's people forget who God is.
Then David arrived.
Not as a soldier.
Not as a king.
Not as a celebrity.
Not as a prophet.
Just a shepherd carrying food.
Nobody expected history to change that day.
Yet God often enters ordinary moments through ordinary people.
David heard the same giant.
Saw the same battlefield.
Faced the same circumstances.
But he asked a different question.
"Who is this uncircumcised Philistine?"
The Hebrew text uses the word עָרֵל (arel), meaning uncircumcised.
This was not merely an insult.
David was identifying covenant reality.
Everyone else saw size.
David saw separation from God.
Everyone else saw military strength.
David saw spiritual weakness.
Everyone else measured the giant against themselves.
David measured the giant against God.
That changed everything.
David's question was really asking:
"Why are we afraid of someone who stands outside the covenant promises of the Lord?"
That perspective shattered me.
Because I realized how often I do exactly what Israel did.
I look at financial giants.
Health giants.
Family giants.
Addictions.
Failures.
Regrets.
Broken dreams.
Closed doors.
Criticism.
Rejection.
And I spend more time studying the giant than remembering God.
Israel had forgotten something.
The giant was loud.
But God was bigger.
The giant was visible.
But God was greater.
The giant was intimidating.
But God was sovereign.
David understood what many believers still forget.
Victory begins with perspective.
The giant did not fall because David had a sling.
The giant fell because David had faith.
Before a stone ever left his hand, the battle had already been settled in his heart.
When David confronted Goliath, he declared:
"You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin, but I come to you in the name of the LORD of hosts..." (1 Samuel 17:45)
The Hebrew name used here is יְהוָה צְבָאוֹת (YHWH Tseva'ot).
"The LORD of Hosts."
"The Lord of Heaven's Armies."
David was not walking onto a battlefield alone.
He was walking with confidence in the God who commands every power in heaven and earth.
This is where the story becomes personal.
Because many of us know what it feels like to stand before giants.
Some giants wear the face of shame.
Some wear the face of addiction.
Some wear the face of depression.
Some wear the face of betrayal.
Some wear the face of past mistakes that still haunt us years later.
Some wear the face of scandals we wish nobody knew about.
Maybe you know that feeling.
The feeling of believing your failures are bigger than your future.
The feeling of believing your sin is stronger than God's mercy.
The feeling of believing your story is already ruined.
That is exactly why the Gospel is such astonishing news.
Because the greatest lesson from David's question is not ultimately about giants.
It is about Jesus.
David points beyond himself.
Like so many stories in Scripture, this one whispers the coming of a greater King.
David stepped onto a battlefield where nobody else could win.
Jesus stepped into a world where nobody else could save.
David fought a giant threatening God's people.
Jesus defeated sin, death, and hell threatening all humanity.
David won victory for Israel.
Jesus won eternal victory for everyone who believes.
The Greek New Testament declares:
"Tetelestai" (Τετέλεσται).
"It is finished." (John 19:30)
Not "it has started."
Not "it might happen."
Not "try harder."
Finished.
Completed.
Accomplished.
Paid in full.
At the cross, Jesus confronted the giant every human being ultimately faces.
Sin.
The Hebrew word often used is חַטָּאת (chatta'th), meaning missing the mark.
Every one of us has missed the mark.
Every one of us has fallen short.
Every one of us carries a story stained by failure.
Yet the Gospel is the story of God entering scandal and transforming it into grace.
Look throughout Scripture.
Moses was a murderer.
Rahab was a prostitute.
Peter denied Christ.
Paul persecuted Christians.
David himself committed adultery and arranged a death.
Yet God was not finished writing.
And perhaps that is exactly what you need to hear today.
Your worst chapter is not your final chapter.
The enemy wants you to believe your scandal defines you.
Jesus says His grace can rewrite you.
The enemy points to your past.
Jesus points to His cross.
The enemy says you are disqualified.
Jesus says, "Come to Me."
The enemy says the giant cannot fall.
Jesus says nothing is impossible with God.
That is why our mission has always been simple.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Maybe that is why this story grips the human heart after thousands of years.
Because deep down, we all know what it feels like to stand before something bigger than ourselves.
And deep down, we all long for a Savior greater than our failures.
David's question still echoes through history.
"Who is this uncircumcised Philistine?"
In other words:
"Why are we fearing something that must ultimately answer to God?"
What giant has been stealing your peace?
What fear has been controlling your decisions?
What lie has been shaping your identity?
What failure have you allowed to become your name?
Bring it before Christ.
Not because you are strong.
Because He is.
Not because you are worthy.
Because He is merciful.
Not because your past is clean.
Because His blood is sufficient.
And if this message stirred something in your spirit, do not keep it to yourself.
Someone is losing hope.
Someone is carrying shame.
Someone is wondering whether God could ever forgive them.
What giant has God helped you overcome?
Let believers around the world pray for you.
You will also gain access to exclusive content while helping us continue reaching souls with the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Because one share can reach a hurting soul.
One comment can encourage a struggling believer.
One testimony can point someone to Christ.
And one surrendered life can become a story only God could write.
The giant was never the biggest thing on the battlefield. The God David trusted was.
